Launcher: Red Two opens on its settings (the same pages as the in-game menu) before the game starts. Start game (the first row) or the controller's START launches it. Turn off "Show launcher at start" there to go straight into the game from then on; the in-game menu (F1 or Back) has the same switch and "Back to launcher". --launcher / --no-launcher override the setting for one start. A reset from the menu goes straight back into the game.

Gamepads work through SDL (with rumble), also while the window is in the background. On an Xbox-style pad the face buttons follow the GameCube positions: A = A (fire), X (left) = B, B (right) = X, Y = Y; LT/RT = L/R, RB = Z, right stick = C-stick, Menu = Start. Keyboard: WASD or arrows steer, Space = A (fire), Left Shift = B, E = X, Q = Y, R = Z, 1/2 = L/R, Enter = Start, IJKL = C-stick, TFGH = D-pad.

estado.texto: The default LLE-first build boots, renders, plays audio, completes the attract demo, starts a new game, traverses doors, pauses, and saves at Samus's ship. It remains a work in progress and needs broader end-to-end regression testing.

bloques: The pinned shared framework uses cached HLE frame composition by default on Windows x64. This host presentation optimization is separate from the guest CPU's LLE scheduler and optional game-routine HLE described below. The existing CPU, audio and status interfaces remain intact. Build the maintained correctness-reference compositor separately with cmake -S . -B build-frame-lle -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSNESRECOMP_FRAME_IMPL=LLE, then cmake --build build-frame-lle. Selection is fixed at build time. LLE can reduce performance; it remains available for correctness checks. Other platforms keep…

The reviewed native-view, uncapped Windows route measured 427.737 to 1259.308 FPS (+194.41%, process CPU -66.67%); it includes boot/menu work and natural demo play. The owner accepted the normal-paced adaptive HLE build. These figures describe that measured build/route, not a new measurement of later upstream title changes or other platforms. Foreign compiler activity limits precision. Normal play retains normal pacing/audio. See the shared framework's frame model.

LLE-first recompilation of Super Metroid (SNES) into native C, using the snesrecomp framework. This repo is the per-game side: the single-fiber runtime, the per-game .cfg, the build glue, and optional HLE optimizations. The recompiled C output (src/gen/, ~93 MB) is generated locally and is not committed.
This is game #4 on snesrecomp, after Mega Man X, Super Mario World, and The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past.

The ROM and interpreter are the architectural ground truth. Proven hot 65816 functions may be statically translated to C, while every absent or rejected exact M/X variant executes the original ROM through LLE. HLE is an optional optimization over that model. The rest of the SNES is not recompiled — it's hardware: PPU rendering, the APU/SPC700 audio coprocessor, DMA and HDMA channels, hardware register I/O, and bank-mapping all run through the embedded SNES emulation in snesrecomp/runner/src/snes/. Recompile the CPU, emulate the silicon.
The default LLE scheduler executes the real WaitForNMI loop and resumes at its architectural continuation. Optional HLE mode replaces that wait with a host-fiber yield for performance.
The ROM is never redistributed — you supply your own legally-dumped copy.

The default LLE-first build boots, renders, plays audio, completes the attract demo, starts a new game, traverses doors, pauses, and saves at Samus's ship. It remains a work in progress and needs broader end-to-end regression testing.

Session logs and gameplay replay capture are enabled automatically, including after an update. No diagnostic mod or console setup is needed. When a problem occurs, stop playing and quit normally if possible. Zip the session's logs/sm-*.log and all matching logs/sm-replay-* files: .replay, .replay.sav, .replay.config.ini and .replay.mods.txt. A .replay alone is insufficient. Attach last_run_report.json and any crash_report_*.json or crash_minidump_*.dmp files too, before launching the game again. Include your release version, OS, what happened and roughly when. Keep your ROM out of the ZIP.

BT4decomp Budokai Tenkaichi 4 B14 Rev2. Native desktop runtime. Simultaneous team battles. Online Tag Team, tournaments, spectator rooms and proximity voice, built on Tenkaichi3Decomp. Join the official Discord community for matchmaking, project news and support.
Download · Install · Documentation · Report an issue

BT4decomp adapts BT4 B14 Rev2 for Windows, Linux and Apple Silicon. It runs the game code natively rather than emulating a console. Installation requires your own compatible Spanish or English BT4 ISO; disc images and extracted game data are not distributed here.
Windows security review in progress. Users reported antivirus alerts for the R5 package. See the investigation and executable hashes.

Game menus support English and Spanish, with an optional Brazilian Portuguese pack. Setup supports English, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese. F1 settings support English, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese. F1 > Spectator offers free camera, fighter tracking and fight overview, with target, speed, zoom and reset controls. Keyboard and controller camera input replaces local fighter input while the camera is active; Start remains available. Panoramic mode expands menus and HUD across the viewport. Hiding the combat HUD also dismisses the Start pause menu; press Start to open it again.

Proximity voice Talk across both teams, with volume adjusted by fighter distance. Choose microphone and output devices, voice activation, threshold and playback volume. Display controls Windows offers Vulkan, native Direct3D 11, Direct3D 12 and OpenGL. Adjust render scale, aspect ratio, effects and motion presentation independently of combat simulation. Custom content Add compatible stages with matching PNG previews, or install custom music. See the stage guide and music guide .

F1 > Mods manages the included Modern HUD, Modern Camera, Modern Look and Skill List scripts. Mods start disabled. Each player can choose their own presentation settings; existing scripts and settings are preserved by automatic updates. F1 > Controls selects one target control method: L3, the right stick or the D-pad. F1 > Spectator can keep the normal camera during special attacks. See the Lua mod guide. F1 > Tech offers optional mechanics adjustments for offline duels; online matches, Tag Team and replays retain their original rules.
Download your platform's ZIP from the latest published release and extract it completely.
Run BT4decomp-setup.exe on Windows, or ./BT4decomp-setup on Linux and macOS.
Select the setup language, game language and your compatible BT4 B14 Rev2 ISO.
Start BT4decomp.exe on Windows, or ./BT4decomp on Linux and macOS. Language installation and setup preview

A single-language installation opens directly in that language. Selecting both languages downloads the alternate package from this repository and enables language selection at startup. Public language and HD texture packages download without GitHub sign-in.
For Linux permissions, macOS download handling and source builds, see native platform setup. Intel Macs and Linux ARM are not targets of these packages.

Open F1 > Updates > Check for updates to look for a new version. The game also checks this repository automatically for the latest signed package for its platform. It verifies the archive SHA-256 and Ed25519 signature, then asks for a game restart to apply the update at the offline main menu. Saves, settings, installed game data and custom content remain outside the replacement list. Updating does not restart an active battle or online session.
Installations that predate the signed updater need one initial package installation. Subsequent published signed updates can install through the launcher.

Konami's 1989 arcade game Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles as a native game for computers, the Nintendo Switch, Android and Anbernic's handhelds, built on its decompilation, tmntarcade-decomp: the game's programs in C, checked frame by frame against MAME in state, picture and sound. Two games come out of it:
TMNT Arcade: the arcade game as it is: coins, the test mode, four players.
TMNT: the console version, the arcade game made for playing at home.
This repository contains no game data: you bring your own ROM set (MAME's tmnt, World 4 Players), and the game takes its assets out of it.

Download the package for Windows, Linux or macOS from the releases (on macOS TMNT Arcade comes in a package of its own, tmnt-arcade-macos-universal.zip). Keep tmnt.zip beside the game, or drop it on its window when it asks: the first time, it takes the assets out of it.

Each device has a package of its own, its games without assets (Android's, when the release signs them), ready to take them out of your tmnt.zip on the device, beside the tool that makes your own of them on a computer (for Windows, macOS and Linux):
Nintendo Switch (tmnt-switch.zip): TMNT.nro and TMNT Arcade.nro for the Homebrew Menu, with tmnt.zip in /switch/tmnt/ on the SD card; or TMNT NSP makes TMNT.nsp and TMNT Arcade.nsp for the HOME menu.

Android (tmnt-android.zip): TMNT APK makes TMNT.apk and TMNT Arcade.apk with the assets inside, signed with a key of yours (ports/android/apk); a release signed with the project's key also has them in ready/, without assets, with tmnt.zip in the app's folder. Phones, tablets, and TVs with Android TV or Google TV (the Chromecast with Google TV too: its Android is 32-bit, and the APKs have both kinds), in the TV's apps with a banner.
Anbernic's H700 handhelds (tmnt-anbernic.zip, RG40XX H...): the folder for PORTS, with tmnt.zip in PORTS/tmnt/; or TMNT Anbernic makes it with the assets inside.
What a tool makes has the game's data in it: it is yours alone, never share it. Each package's README.txt says how.

The pre-release testing, in the releases too, has the next release's changes for the players to try before it comes out: made again at each change from the branch testing, TMNT's OPTIONS showing which (V1.0.7-TEST1). It may not work yet; what you find goes in the issues.

ARCADE: the arcade's game with no coins: START brings a player in at any time, up to four, and on a continue lets him pick his turtle again. With OPTIONS > COINS, with them, as the cabinet: keys 5 to 8 or a controller's Back put a player's coin in.
SPLINTER WAY: NORMAL (5 lives and 3 continues), BOSS RUSH (from one boss to the next, 5 lives and no continues) and RONIN (one turtle against the enemies of a four-player game).
MULTIPLAYER: up to four computers on the local network in one game (below).

OPTIONS: controls for four players, difficulty, lives, coins, demo sound, region (the NINJA or HERO title), video (window, full screen, sharp, smooth, bilinear or CRT pixels, integer scale, WIDE 16:10, 16:9 or 20:9, VSYNC, FPS, PRESS START blinking, still or off), volume, sound test.
The pause in a game: CONTINUE, RESTART, QUIT GAME.
The attract mode: the arcade's own (its story, the demos, the profiles) after the presentation, and after 30 seconds on the menu with nothing pressed; any key or button opens the menu.
And the Konami code on the menu.

Keyboard: the arrows move, Z or left Ctrl attacks, X or left Alt jumps, C does both at once (the special attack), Enter is START; Escape pauses (and goes back in the menus). F11 or Alt+Enter is the full screen, F3 the next kind of pixels. OPTIONS > CONTROLS changes each player's keys and buttons.

bloques: Pokémon Emerald, reimagined as a Square Enix HD-2D game.

This is Pokémon Emerald with a lit, depth-blurred 3D diorama look, running natively on the Steam Deck and on Windows. It is the same game and the same saves. The decompiled game is compiled to a 32-bit program, and a small layer on SDL2 and OpenGL stands in for the GBA hardware, so it is not an emulator.
The repository holds no game data. You build the game yourself from a dump of your own cartridge, and the result is for your own use. Please do not share builds, since they contain Nintendo's data.
The new title screen. Littleroot Town.
A battle, with the backdrop blurred. Before (left) and after (right).

The easiest way is the builder, a small program in the look of Windows 95. It carries this repository inside it, so you only need your ROM and an internet connection. It downloads the build tools and the game files, builds the game, and puts it in the folder you chose. Nothing is uploaded.
Download it from the latest release: BravelyEmeraldBuilder-win.zip for Windows, or the .tar.gz for Linux and SteamOS (then run sh install.sh).
Pick a folder to build in.
Tick the box that allows the downloads and press Build.

The first build downloads the compiler tools and takes 30 to 60 minutes, and it needs about 15 GB of disk space. More in docs/BUILDER.md. To build by hand, see docs/BUILD_DECK.md for the Steam Deck and docs/WINDOWS_BUILD.md for Windows.
Lighting: a real sun shadow map, soft shadows under characters, and sun and moon rays that follow the time of day.
Depth blur that follows the scene, plus bloom, colour grading and a vignette.
Relief on the ground, walls and sprites, so flat pixel art picks up a sense of depth.
Wind in the trees and grass, tall grass that bends as you walk, flowers, and water glints.
Weather and particles: rain with streaks, mist, splashes and wet ground, pollen, fireflies, leaves.
Ambient sound that fits the place: wind, rain, waves, crickets, birds, cave drips, thunder.
Battles on a blurred 3D backdrop, with a coloured flash and glow when a move hits.
Glass panels, smoother menus and bars, and button icons that match the Deck.
A new title screen and an intro that reveals the HD-2D picture from the flat GBA one.
Every effect has its own setting (off, low, medium, high) in the in-game options menu. With all of them off you get the old picture back.
Full feature and settings list: docs/FEATURES.md

It works on the Steam Deck and on Windows. The Linux builder has not been tried on real hardware yet, and some things have not been checked on every machine. Reports and issues are welcome. The list of known problems is in docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md.

Konami's 1991 arcade game The Simpsons as a native game for computers, the Nintendo Switch, Android, iPhone and iPad, and Anbernic's handhelds, built on its decompilation, simpsons-decomp: both of the game's programs (the Konami 053248's and the Z80's) in C, checked frame by frame against MAME in state, picture and sound. Two games come out of it:
The Simpsons Arcade Game: the arcade game as it is: coins, the test mode, four players.
The Simpsons Mr. Plow Edition: the console version, the arcade game made for playing at home.

This repository contains no game data: you bring your own ROM set (MAME's simpsons, 4 Players World, set 1), and the game takes its assets out of it. Only that set: MAME's other sets of the game (the 2 Players ones, the Japanese and Asian ones) have program ROMs of their own, which the decompilation does not cover, and the game refuses them.

Download the package for Windows, Linux or macOS from the releases. Keep simpsons.zip beside the game, or drop it on its window when it asks: the first time, it takes the assets out of it (simpsons.assets, a fraction of a second), and plays from them from then on (simpsons.7z, the set packed by 7-Zip, works too). A shortcut or a launcher can name it instead, with --game PATH (the .zip, the .7z, or its folder); --prepare makes the assets with no window and ends. RecompLauncher sets The Simpsons Mr. Plow Edition up this way, from the release's recomplauncher.json, and shows OPTIONS' settings on…
Each device has a package of its own, its games without assets, beside the tools that make your own of them on a computer (for Windows, macOS and Linux):

Nintendo Switch (simpsons-switch.zip): The Simpsons Mr. Plow Edition.nro and The Simpsons Arcade Game.nro for the Homebrew Menu, with simpsons.zip in /switch/simpsons-arcade/ on the SD card; or Simpsons NSP makes The Simpsons Mr. Plow Edition.nsp and The Simpsons Arcade Game.nsp for the HOME menu.

Android (simpsons-android.zip): Simpsons APK makes The Simpsons Mr. Plow Edition.apk and The Simpsons Arcade Game.apk on your computer, with the assets of your simpsons.zip inside, signed with a key of yours (ports/android/apk). Phones, tablets, foldables, and TVs with Android TV or Google TV (in the TV's apps, with a banner; the APKs carry 32-bit ARM too, for the Chromecast with Google TV).

iPhone and iPad (simpsons-ios.zip): unsigned .ipa files to install with AltStore, SideStore or Sideloadly, and simpsons.zip put in the game's folder with the Files app or the Finder. They are not, and will not be, on the App Store.
Anbernic's H700 handhelds (simpsons-anbernic.zip, the stock firmware): the folder for PORTS, with simpsons.zip in PORTS/simpsons/; or Simpsons Anbernic makes it with the assets inside.
What a tool makes has the game's data in it: it is yours alone, never share it. Each package's README.txt says how.
The Konami presentation: the family walks across the game's own big Konami logo, then Bart has a word.
The menu on the TV: the family's TV from the attract mode, the title on its screen.

ARCADE: the arcade's game with no coins: each player picks a character on the game's own portraits, one each, and START brings a player in at any time, up to four. After a continue, or for a new player, START picks again. OPTIONS sets its lives and its continues (0 to 9, or UNLIMITED).
FREE PLAY: the arcade game from stage 1, as many continues as you like.
BOSS RUSH: the bosses one after another, from the wrestler to Mr. Burns, each stage crossed to its boss out of sight.
BONUS GAMES: the two bonus stages in a row, for one to four players, with their results.
FRANK GRIMES LIFE: one player, the whole game, against what four players would face.

bloques: A native PC port of Conker's Bad Fur Day (N64, US version). It's built by statically recompiling the game with N64Recomp, starting from the Conker decompilation. It runs on N64ModernRuntime and is rendered by RT64.
This repository contains no game data. You need your own legally obtained copy of the US ROM. Everything from the game is extracted from that ROM on your machine during the build.

Ready-to-play Windows, Linux and macOS (Apple Silicon, macOS 15 or later) builds are on the Releases page. Unpack one anywhere, run ConkerRecomp, and pick your US ROM in the launcher the first time. The packages contain no game data: you still need your own ROM. The macOS app isn't signed with an Apple developer ID, so the first time, open it and then choose Open Anyway in System Settings > Privacy & Security. To build it yourself instead, read on.

Runs natively on Windows (Direct3D 12 or Vulkan), Linux (Vulkan) and macOS (Metal), rendered by RT64. Supports higher resolutions, widescreen, anti-aliasing and high frame-rate presentation, with Conker, his shadow and the camera interpolated between the game's frames.

Widescreen across gameplay, menus, cutscenes (or 4:3 cutscenes, with the Cutscene Aspect Ratio option), split screen and the pause screen, with the world drawn and culled for the wider view. Overscan Borders hides the N64's black border down each side.

Game controllers and keyboard, with remappable controls (mouse buttons too) and rumble settings (motor, style and strength). N64 pads and adapters for real N64 controllers are built in, and each controller gets its own player in multiplayer.
Mouse and gyro aiming, a free camera on the right stick (or the mouse) that stays out of walls, camera turning speed and inversion, and a Field of View setting.

An aiming Reticle, a green ring like Live & Reloaded's, and Swap Sticks and Lock-On options for aiming. With Swap Sticks, Conker walks while aiming, the sniper scope included (zooming with the D-pad or the mouse wheel).
Full audio: music, sound effects and the voice acting, each with a volume of its own (Music, Sound Effects and Speech, under the Main Volume).
A launcher with settings, controls and a mod menu (RecompFrontend, as in Zelda 64: Recompiled and Banjo: Recompiled).
The game's reflective surfaces (Conker's glass, the logo's sheen) and its point lights (the bar's lantern, the N64 logo), drawn as on the N64.
Conker's Detail keeps Conker on his most detailed model, and Show FPS puts a frame rate counter in the corner.
Shadows ease toward the light they're cast from, instead of snapping about with flickering lights.
Achievements, the program's own, for reaching the game's scenes.
ROM hacks that only change the game's assets, such as the uncensored ROM and the Russian, German and Brazilian Portuguese translations, with the launcher switching between them.
Mod support (.nrm mods: function patches and hooks). Three mods are included: Skip Intro, Skip Any Cutscene and Cheats.
Texture packs (RT64's .rtz, and GLideN64's .htc and .hts), for HD textures and other replacements.
Save states: save anywhere with F5 and load with F7, in nine slots (how to use them, and how they work).
Netplay (built with the CMake option CONKER_NETPLAY, off by default): online multiplayer from the launcher's Netplay menu. See Netplay.
The game is playable, and has been played through to the end. Known issues:
Widescreen: the pause menu's blurred background is the 4:3 frame scaled up to the full width, so its top and bottom are cropped.
Only the US ROM is supported (and ROM hacks that only change its assets: see ROM hacks).

An unofficial Windows PC runtime for the NTSC-U 1.1 release of Syphon Filter (SCUS-94240). The project combines the original PlayStation gameplay code with a native Windows host for rendering, input, menus, audio and FMV playback.

This repository does not contain the game or a disc image. A legally obtained BIN/CUE image of the supported release is required. The project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony Interactive Entertainment.
Download the latest Windows x64 build from GitHub Releases. Release-specific changes and checksums are published with each release. See CHANGELOG.md for the aggregate history.
Download SyphonFilterPC- -win64.zip from the release page.
Extract the ZIP into a new folder.
On Launch, select Browse and choose the CUE file for Syphon Filter USA v1.1. Review Graphics and Controls, then select Play.
The single-window launcher also includes the Dossiers gallery. Its complete interface is available in English and Russian.
Keep every BIN file next to its CUE file and do not rename the files referenced by the CUE sheet. The launcher remembers the selected image but never copies it into the game directory.
The runtime validates the executable from the selected image. Other regions, revisions, repacks and modified images are not expected to work.
Original R3000A mission/gameplay execution with native Windows presentation.
Complete 20-mission campaign flow, checkpoint restore and persistent mission unlock progress.
Modular single-window launcher with Launch, Graphics, Controls and Dossiers tabs. The complete launcher UI is available in English and Russian and keeps all settings staged until Play.
Configurable internal resolution, aspect mode, fullscreen, frame pacing, texture filtering, SMAA/MSAA and optional volumetric particle effects.

Optional Russian text pack for all 20 missions, menus, briefings, weapon descriptions and baked map labels, with a unified Industry Bold 2x pixel atlas matching the original Industria-style interface for Latin and Cyrillic text. Speech, music and FMV remain sourced from the selected USA v1.1 image and are never replaced.
Remappable keyboard/mouse controls and retail-style gamepad controls.
Native OpenAL presentation of game audio and FFmpeg-backed PS1 STR playback.
High-resolution, perspective-correct and Z-buffered scene rendering with PGXP geometry support.

Dynamic scene lighting layered over the authored PS1 vertex colours: intact mission lamps, fire, alternating police lights, muzzle flashes, explosions and the retail flashlight illuminate terrain, props and actors with bounded falloff and surface-aware response. Gabe, allies and enemies cast posed, light-directed shadows onto authored floors, slopes and moving lifts.
Restored PS1-style HUD, inventory, objectives, parameters, weapons and map pages, including current-position and active-objective indicators.
Correct scene occlusion for pickups, grenade sprites and transient effects.
Weapon muzzle flashes for player and enemy weapons, with first-person behavior matching the current camera mode.
Restored glass/window destruction shards and restart-safe destructible state.
Integrated Dossiers tab with four sharpened bonus pages.

The implementation is still a public test. Gameplay remains driven by the guest runtime; rendering, platform integration and selected presentation systems are native. Bug reports should include the mission number, reproduction steps, GPU, screenshot and the generated log, but never a BIN/CUE image.
Saves and launcher settings are stored outside the installation directory:

A native PC (Windows and Linux) port of the 1997 PlayStation action game Disney's Hercules (all five PAL releases: English, French, German, Italian, Spanish), plus the decompilation work behind it. The game logic runs unchanged as statically recompiled code; only the platform layer is replaced: 1080p, true 16:9, HD sprites, level textures and HUD, a CRT simulation, save states, and a launcher styled after the game's own title menus (in German, English, French, Spanish and Italian) that boots straight into the level you pick.

This repository contains no game data. You need your own copy of the game. Every graphic, sound and code byte of the game is read from your disc image at build or run time, and everything made from it (extracted files, disassembly, HD texture packs, launcher artwork) stays out of git. The prebuilt downloads contain the game's program code translated to x86-64, but no graphics, sound, video or level data: those still come from your disc. The optional HD texture packs (upscaled from the game's graphics) are published separately as the hd-packs release; the launcher can also make them from your…
Fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Disney or Sony.
Prebuilt for players who don't want to build it themselves:
Checksums and release notes: latest release.
Unzip into a folder of its own (the archive has no top-level folder).

On first start, pick your disc image (.cue + .bin, .chd, .bin, .img or .iso) of one of the PAL releases SCES-00891 (English), -00892 (French), -00893 (German), -00894 (Italian) or -00895 (Spanish). The US release (SLUS-01029) is not supported. The launcher's language picks the release; it asks for that release's disc and remembers it (disc.cfg, disc- .cfg) next to the program.
Choose a level in the launcher. Keyboard, mouse and gamepads work; F11 toggles fullscreen.
In the game, Esc (gamepad: Select + Start) opens the menu: HD on/off, CRT picture, 16:9 or 4:3, volume, the controls and more, all switched live. Every key is listed in CONTROLS.md.
Windows shows a SmartScreen warning because the program is not signed: click More info → Run anyway.

Updates come by themselves (from 0.5.0 on): on start the launcher checks for a new release, shows its changelog and installs it on request. Settings, saves, the disc path and the HD graphics stay. Options → General → Auto updates turns the check off. Coming from 0.4.0 or older: unzip the new download over your existing folder once, so your HD graphics and saves stay.

HD graphics are downloaded after your first game (from 0.5.1 on): the launcher fetches the pack for your release from the hd-packs release in the background, about 1.6 GB, checked against SHA256SUMS.txt; a second language then only needs the difference, a few to 40 MB. The progress shows on the main menu and under Options → Graphics → HD graphics; once done, HD is switched on.

If that release has no pack for your disc, the launcher makes the pack on your PC, from your disc, at low priority: about 4 hours on a laptop CPU, while you play in the original graphics. It stops when you close the launcher and continues on the next start. For this it downloads, once, about 400 MB from the official sources, each checked against a fixed SHA-256: a portable Python (python-build-standalone), PyTorch (CPU), spandrel and chaiNNer's image helpers, and the upscaling models from their authors' releases (IllustrationJaNai, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; HDcube). It needs 6 GB of free disk space…

TPVR is a vibecoded VR mod for Dusklight, the PC of Twilight Princess. It is not affiliated with the Dusklight team in any way.
It aims to be as accurate as possible to the original game while allowing you to experience the gameplay from a VR perspective.
More on why it uses AI generated code below.
Physical sword swinging, shield bashing and aiming (aim with the right hand)
Quest 2/3 controller bindings; other headsets are untested
The ability to play the game in flatscreen for parts you want to skip in VR
[!IMPORTANT] TPVR does not provide any copyrighted assets. You must provide your own copy of the original game.

[!IMPORTANT] At a minimum, TPVR requires a GPU with support for D3D12. It is only supported on Windows so far. Your experience with specific hardware, operating systems, VR software and drivers may vary. Virtual Desktop with VDXR is your best bet at the moment.
You must dump your own copy of the game. Please see this article for instructions. After dumping, you can use a program like Dolphin or nodtool to convert the .iso to .rvz to save space.
Dusklight currently supports all commercial discs except for Wii's Korean release.

[!NOTE] Dusklight is based on the Twilight Princess decompilation, which is currently only matching for GameCube. As a result, even when playing Dusklight with a Wii disc, you will be presented with the GameCube version's HUD and certain other specificities.
Download the latest release, extract the zip file, and run Dusklight.exe with your choice of VR streamer open.
If you'd like to build TPVR from source, please read the build instructions.

Expand I do not know how to code. The furthest my knowledge goes is a little bit of HTML and CSS. I simply wanted a way to play Twilight Princess in VR and scoured the internet for anyone who mentioned a Dusklight mod/port in the works, but came up with nothing, so I decided to take matters into my own hands with Claude Code. This has taken hours of almost daily work in the last 3 weeks.

I do not condone the usage of AI for writing, "art", deepfakes, and music (especially music, screw Suno and its garbage that is polluting streaming services). It should not be people's go-to for asking questions or replacing a search engine; it has repeatedly been shown to hallucinate and take certain statements out of context, spreading misinformation. It should be used as a tool and you must guide that tool.

With that being said, for a task like this, I believe it is acceptable to create a project that does not currently exist by writing the code using AI as long as you actually take the time to refine the experience and do not harm other people's repos or code in the process. In this case, I simply forked Dusklight and modified it in a separate instance over the course of multiple weeks, without pestering the devs with possible spaghetti-code pull requests. I wrote this statement and edited the README in my own words, and I made the logo using Paint.NET despite having very little graphic design…

I have seen many recent projects spring up in the same vein: vibecoded VR ports of existing games. Everybody is entitled to their own opinion, and different backgrounds will lead people to take different stances. However, I believe that you can either take this VR port of the original game and enjoy it for what it is, regardless of AI or not, or you can simply ignore it and play the game in flatscreen—it's still a fantastic experience.
And yes—I used an em-dash there. You can type it with on your keyboard with Alt+0151. Thanks ChatGPT for ruining informal basic writing.

estado.texto: Playable on Windows: both discs, movies, music and sound, saves, controllers. It plays as the console does and adds what a PC can, all optional:

bloques: PE2PC: Parasite Eve II, native on PC

A native PC port of Parasite Eve II (PlayStation, USA release) built on the decompilation by GabeRealB. The game's own code, decompiled to C, is compiled for the PC and runs natively; a small runtime written for this project stands in for the console (graphics, sound, CD, controllers, memory cards). No emulator and no code from Sony.
This repository contains no game data. To play, you need dumps of your own discs (SLUS-01042 and SLUS-01055, as .chd or .cue images). The port reads the game's data from them at run time.

[!IMPORTANT] Dumps of the original USA release work, and the Brazilian Portuguese fan translation's discs. The port is built from the decompilation of that exact release, so it expects its code byte for byte. The Brazilian Portuguese translation keeps that code and changes only texts and pictures, so its discs play as they are, with the high-definition text too. Other regions (European, Japanese), other fan translations, and patched, hacked or otherwise modified images are not supported and will not run correctly. Translations and other changes go in as mods instead (see docs/MODDING.md).
Playable on Windows: both discs, movies, music and sound, saves, controllers. It plays as the console does and adds what a PC can, all optional:
Higher resolution, up to 8x the console's 320x240, rendered on the graphics card, with exact (sub-pixel) vertex positions so models neither wobble nor crack, and perspective-correct textures.
Smooth motion at 60 fps: the game still runs at its 30, and frames in between are drawn with the 3D models halfway, with no added delay.
Filtering: smoothed 3D textures (bilinear) and smoothly enlarged pre-rendered backgrounds (bicubic).
Presentation: a CRT look (scanlines and aperture grille) and integer scaling.
Modern movement: the stick points where to go, relative to the camera, in exploration and in battle; or the original tank controls with a quick turn (back + run).

Sharp text: the dialogue, the menus, the loading captions and the disc change's lines drawn from high-definition fonts (the built-in DejaVu Sans Bold, Hind Bold and Courier Prime) instead of the game's small pictures of text, at internal resolutions above the console's; the speakers' names over the dialogue too, in any language a translation gives them.

Quality of life, each optional and off by default (the launcher's QoL tab, or the pause menu's Options > Gameplay): faster camera changes and doors, skipping the intro, dialogue shown whole at once, item boxes that share their contents, 30 inventory spaces, a full inventory's pickups and battle winnings sent to the box, identical medicines stacked, and saving from the pause menu wherever the game lets you move freely. Item boxes also sort their contents.

Mods (experimental, turned on in Settings): replace the pre-rendered backgrounds and full-screen pictures and the textures with your own at any resolution, the music with recordings, the movies with video files, any of the game's files, and its texts with translations (the dialogue, the menus, the items' details); cheats and memory patches; the game's pictures, textures, music, movies, files and texts extracted from your discs with pe2 --extract, filed in folders by what they are, to make them; translations imported from translated discs, their translated pictures and loading captions…
Cheats (in pe2.toml, [cheats]): infinite HP or MP, one-hit kills, every hit critical, and EXP and BP multipliers.

Comfort: a launcher worked by mouse, keyboard or controller (English or Portuguese), remappable keys and controller buttons, pause, screenshots, borderless full screen, and Discord showing where you are in the game, with your EXP and BP.
Memory cards are raw .mcd images, so saves move both ways with DuckStation.

Orre Launcher (formerly Colosseum Launcher) sets up and plays the native PC port of Pokémon Colosseum, and of Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness, on Windows, macOS, and Linux. The launcher guides you through setup, downloads the tools it needs, and gives you one big Play button when you're ready.
Bring your own game. You need a disc image made from your own North American Pokémon Colosseum disc (or Pokémon XD disc, GXXE01, for XD). The launcher does not include a game or disc image.
This is an unofficial fan project, not affiliated with Nintendo, Creatures, GAME FREAK or The Pokémon Company.
Download Orre Launcher from the latest release
The launcher requires a 64-bit computer and an internet connection for setup. Required setup tools download automatically.
Open the .exe installer and follow the steps, then open the launcher. Its files and shortcuts are still named Colosseum Launcher.

Portable version: put Colosseum-Launcher- -win-portable.exe in any folder, such as on a USB drive, and open it. Nothing is installed. The first time it runs, it creates a Colosseum-Launcher-Portable folder next to the .exe and keeps everything there: settings, setup files, build tools, the game, saves, and save backups. Portable versions don't update themselves: to update, put the new portable .exe in place of the old one, next to the same folder.
Drag Colosseum Launcher.app onto Applications in the window that opens.
Eject the disk image, then open it from Applications.
Download the .AppImage, allow it to run as a program in your file manager's permissions settings, then open it.
The launcher walks you through three steps:
Download setup files. Use the suggested location, or choose a different folder before downloading.

Choose disc image. Select a copy of your own original North American Pokémon Colosseum disc: GC6E01, revision 0. Supported files are .iso and .gcm. Compressed formats (CISO, RVZ, GCZ) need converting to ISO first, which Dolphin does with Convert File. The bonus disc is not the game.
Begin setup. The launcher downloads HD textures and builds the game on your computer. This first setup can take a while.

For Pokémon XD, click XD's side of the Play page first. Each game has its own setup folder, disc and memory card: XD saves to colo-port/xd/card-a beside Colosseum's colo-port/card-a, and an XD save already on Colosseum's card moves there by itself (backed up first). XD is early: it plays with the renderer, display, controller, widescreen, HD text, fast-forward and Skip movies settings, and Online; Colosseum's other extras stay hidden while XD is chosen.

On Mac, setup may ask you to install Apple's Command Line Tools. Follow Mac setup help in the launcher. The game is built for your Mac: on Apple Silicon, Beta's game is a native program that draws with Metal, with no Rosetta needed. Stable's game still runs through Rosetta, and setup asks for it.
The progress bar shows what's happening. View build log opens more detail; closing that view keeps setup running. When setup finishes, press Play.
After setup, the main screen is just Play and the tabs above it.
Gameplay skips the movies and chooses how the game's text is drawn.
Display has the screen format, fullscreen, frame rate (30 or 60 fps) and V-Sync.

Graphics has presets (Low, Medium, High, Ultra and Steam Deck), the renderer (Vulkan or OpenGL, and Metal on Apple Silicon, where it is the default), picture sharpness up to 4×, anti-aliasing, filtering, upscaling, the HD textures and HD models.
Controls sets the keys and controller buttons for each GameCube button, and the sticks, triggers and rumble.
Manage game has game updates, rebuilding, the setup folder and disc file, and space cleanup.
The most tracks, most cups, split screen, up to 4p multiplayer, HD mode 7, for F-Zero.
F-Zero Forever is a modern PC conversion of the original SNES anti-gravity racer.
Rather than a predictable port of the game, our ambition was to push the game to new heights, with overwhelming amounts of modes and content, and all the technical improvements we could throw at it.

Our team consists of veteran developers from the RetroPortingToolkit team, and F-Zero modders from the F-Zero Community Grand Prix team. For this special game, we spent over 7 weeks working on new features, daily.
Install the signed APK from the Android and Linux release, then choose your own unmodified F-Zero (USA) .sfc or .smc ROM. No ROM is included.

The Android launcher has native Home, Settings and Mods pages, touch controls and standard gamepad support. Fit to screen and adaptive widescreen default on, with saved choices retained. Android Back opens pause, quick save/load and return to launcher. Portable HD rendering is optional and defaults off on Android. See Android features and building.

We worked with the community and combined several of the highest quality rom hacks for the game, including: Community Grand Prix, Astra Velocity, Bower, and MAX. You can even bring your own rom hacks and create your own races. This is the largest combination of tracks EVER for F-Zero.

All bundled ROM hack content is included with explicit permission from its authors and creators. AI was not used in any way to modify the ROM hacks or their content. The inclusion of their work in this project should not be taken as a statement of their views on AI.

We made sure to preserve every custom feature that was built for each GP, including CGP's magnets, jumps, and gravity changes, with selectable gameplay rules and Legend difficulty for another challenge.

Choose from twelve CGP machines: eight additional vehicles and CGP versions of the original four, each with its authored artwork, handling, energy boosts, and exhaust. Explore separate vehicle packs and original-car rebalances, or enable the optional Satellaview machines!

All twelve cars are enabled by default for fresh single-player settings. Existing profiles keep their saved choices; enable Mods > CGP vehicles to add the eight extra cars. Local and online VS always offer all twelve.

We have also added multiplayer! You can play with 2 players via local split-screen, or up to 4 players via online netplay. Each player can compete with their own vehicle, and we made sure that player collisions, bumper traffic, minimaps and race positions work correctly. Configure your players in the launcher, enable Local Multiplayer, then choose VS MODE on the title screen.
Multiplayer supports rollback netcode, LAN discovery, Direct IP, and online lobbies

HD Mode 7 reconstructs the track perspective with finer sampling at 2×, 4×, or 8× detail, optional edge smoothing, and GPU rendering for every local player. Start at 2× when tuning performance; higher settings are more demanding.

Pair it with 16:9, 21:9, 32:9, or Fit widescreen modes, or keep the classic 4:3 view. Presentation rates from 60 to 360 FPS give high-refresh displays smoother motion, independently of the HD Mode 7 setting.
Room to see the next corner: Forest III in widescreen.
Visuals are upgraded too: it supports any aspect ratio (including 16:9, 21:9, 32:9), unlimited frame rates, and HD Mode 7. It's the prettiest the game has ever looked.
Two racers. Two views. One race.
Online, with the whole screen to yourself

A native LÖVE2D recreation of Poke Red, Blue, Yellow, Gold, Silver, Crystal, FireRed, LeafGreen, Ruby, Sapphire, and Emerald. The engine and map behavior are hand-written Lua; game data and graphics are decoded from a ROM supplied by the player.
And before you say, "that's not a recomp", you're wrong. Recomp is an acronym. Reverse Engineering Causes Obsessive Mental Problems
Click Here for the AI Use Disclosure!

[!CAUTION] We are NOT affiliated with the website gen1recomp[.]com That website is not run by this project, was not authorized by us, and we have no idea who operates it. It is impersonating this project; do not download anything from it, and treat anything it hosts or claims as untrustworthy. Even if the site currently links back to this repository, the people behind it can change its content at any time, so nothing on it should ever be trusted. This GitHub repository, the Discord, and https://gen1re.com are the only official sources for this project. Also, as I assumed would eventually…

G1R Deluxe aka Gen1Recomp is a native LÖVE2D recreation of Pokemon Red, Blue, Yellow, Gold, Silver, Crystal, FireRed, LeafGreen, Ruby, Sapphire, and Emerald. The engine and map behavior are hand-written Lua, ported from the pret disassemblies & C. Game data, graphics, and audio programs are decoded on first launch from a ROM you supply.

The project does not include a ROM, emulate the Game Boy, transpile assembly, or download a disassembly. Your ROM is verified, used during import, and released from memory. It is never copied into the cache, and later launches load the private generated cache without asking for it again. Music, sound effects, and cries are synthesized while the game runs. All eleven games can be imported side by side. Gen 2 support is still under construction.
Download the build for your platform from the latest release.
Launch it. The packaged app contains no ROM and no game data, so the launcher will ask for one.

Choose your legally obtained .gb / .gbc / .gba file, a .zip / .7z that holds one (offered only where your platform's build supports archives), or drop it onto the window. Import takes a few seconds and the game starts automatically.
Repeat for any other game you own. Each one gets its own tab in the launcher.
Only the canonical US English ROMs below are accepted. The importer checks the SHA-1 before creating any game data. FireRed, LeafGreen, Ruby, Sapphire, and Emerald support is in beta.
Platform notes: Linux, iOS, Xbox Dev Mode, handhelds, Nintendo Switch, and PlayStation 4 each have their own install steps.

Windows Defender: it sometimes flags the Windows build with a generic detection such as Trojan:Win32/Wacatac!ml (#621). This is a known false positive: the exe is the official LÖVE runtime with the game archive appended, and Defender distrusts unsigned executables with appended data. Every release publishes sha256sums.txt so you can verify your download, and you can check a flagged file on VirusTotal.
Rebind any of these in-game under OPTIONS > CONTROLS.
COLORS, TILT, ZOOM, SHADER FX, GAME SPEED, and VOID FILL are also in the Options menu and persist in options.lua.

Low-end devices: OPTIONS > PERFORMANCE scales the optional extras for weaker hardware (HIGH, BALANCED, LOW, or AUTO, the default). It only changes presentation; game logic is identical on every tier. Details in docs/new-features.md.
Everything else lives in the docs folder or on the project wiki, which has the modding book, link play, save editor, and developer setup guides:
Rulesets: faithful Gen 1 quirks or modern cleanups
Online play: lobby, battles, tournaments, trading
Launch options: one-click shortcuts and URLs
Portable mode: run from a USB drive

Unofficial native PC ports of Capcom's CPS-2 arcade games (and a CPS-1 one), for macOS, Linux (Steam Deck and ARM64 included), Windows and Android, in one download with one launcher. Each game's program is translated ahead of time into C++ and runs on a machine written for this project, not an emulator. The fighting games add a full training mode, online play with rollback, widescreen and new modes.

No game files are included. You need your own copy of each game: its arcade ROM set (a CPS-2 game's with its key file). Only the versions named below work for each game, and this project cannot help you get one.
Each game's page has all it does, with pictures.
Every fighting game has a full training mode, from the in-game menu (not yet the two classic Street Fighter II games):
Hit boxes (and throw boxes in Alpha 2 and 3), frame data and a frame meter, an input display, and a combo and damage readout (and stun, in the Street Fighter games and Pocket Fighter).

A dummy that stands, crouches or jumps, guards (high, low or after the first hit), techs, gets up quickly, reverses, and records and replays what you show it (each game's page says what its dummy can do).
Health and meter refilled, a stage of your choice, and start over from the round's beginning with one button.
Two players on two machines, or four on up to four in the tag-team games, with rollback netcode. Any mix of macOS, Linux, the Steam Deck and Windows can play each other.

Host a match from the launcher, or from the game you're playing (its menu's Online page: you play on until someone joins), and give the other player its code: they type it on the launcher's Online page. If you've set your name, the match is also listed in the lobby, where anyone can pick it from Online matches. Nothing needs setting up on either router.
The waiting room lists the players whose Online page is open: Invite one to a match in any game, and they Accept from their launcher.

Both players need the same version of CPS-2 Recomp (the launcher shows yours at the top); a match on another version is greyed in the list. Your ROM sets may be different regions of the game: the match is the host's region (best effort: the same set is surest).
Each player presses Start to come in, as at the arcade. The match uses the host's board settings (difficulty, timer, rounds); cheats are off.

Four players: in the tag-team games, with Tag team at 2 vs 2 on the host, a match is four people, each on their own machine or two at a machine (People at this machine on the Online page), all joining with the one code.
Ball battle and tag team online: in two-person matches, the host starts either from the in-game menu (Esc), which opens over the running match, and each player picks their own fighters there.
On screen: the players' names, the ping (and the input delay, if you like), and the win streak of a player who keeps winning.

FT5 / FT10: in Marvel vs. Capcom and X-Men vs. Street Fighter, the host can choose Set format on the Online page before connecting. Everyone sees the team score and the first side to reach the target wins the set. After the participating machines agree on the result, it is shown for two seconds and they return to the launcher.
Watch a match: a host who allows spectators has Watch on its lobby entry once the match is under way. Up to eight viewers follow it, a moment behind, without touching it.

Chat with the other players during a match: press T (or a gamepad's right stick, or the touch screen's Chat) and type, on a keyboard or your system's on-screen keyboard. It goes between the playing machines.
A dropped connection waits for the other player to come back with the same code.

estado.texto: This is an alpha. Please report anything that looks or plays differently from the arcade in Issues, with the log.txt from the game's data folder.

bloques: Virtua Fighter 3 (SEGA, arcade, Model 3, 1996) as a native PC game: the game's own PowerPC program, recompiled to native code, with render scales up to 6x, widescreen and ultrawide, smooth motion up to 120 pictures a second and the 3D on the GPU.
Play · Download · Trailer · Status · Controls · Report a bug

[!IMPORTANT] No game files are included: no ROMs and nothing made from them. You need your own dump of the game as MAME's vf3 set (vf3.zip, Revision D). It is read on your computer, and the game's program is recompiled there each time it starts. An unofficial fan project, not made, approved or supported by SEGA, and not affiliated with it.

Virtua Fighter 3 Recomp runs the game's own program, for the board's PowerPC 603e, recompiled to native code (ARM64 or x86-64) from your ROM each time it starts, and checked frame for frame against its own interpreter, which is itself frame-identical to the Supermodel reference on every scripted run (the attract mode, all twelve fighters, a versus match and the test menu: 173,000 frames). The rest of the Model 3 board is this port's own code: the board itself (memory map, IRQs, the 53C810 SCSI controller's DMA, the JTAG chain, EEPROM, inputs), the tile generator and the Real3D Pro-1000 (a…
This is an alpha. Please report anything that looks or plays differently from the arcade in Issues, with the log.txt from the game's data folder.
Known issues: Shun's stage water is the game's own low-resolution 2D art up close.
Known differences from the reference's pictures: textures far away are softer (the Real3D's own mipmap level choice, as Supermodel's New3D documents it, where the reference build used OpenGL's).
Unzip it (Mac: move Virtua Fighter 3 Recomp to Applications; Windows: the VirtuaFighter3 folder anywhere, not inside Program Files).
Choose your vf3.zip when it asks. A copy is kept, so you only do this once.

Copy the download to the Deck (e.g. Downloads) and unpack it there: in Desktop Mode, right-click it in the file manager > Extract > Extract archive here. (Unpacking on Windows, or copying the folder through a USB stick, can lose the files' permissions, and then nothing launches.)
Put your vf3.zip in the VirtuaFighter3/roms folder.

Desktop Mode: Steam > Games > Add a Non-Steam Game to My Library > Browse, set the file type filter to "All files", pick the vf3 file in the VirtuaFighter3 folder, Add Selected Programs. In its Properties, set Start In to the VirtuaFighter3 folder (e.g. /home/deck/Downloads/VirtuaFighter3/), and under Compatibility leave "Force the use of a specific Steam Play compatibility tool" off: it's a native Linux game, and Proton stops it launching.
Back in Game Mode, launch it from your Library with the default Gamepad layout.

The Windows download also runs on the Deck under Proton (add VirtuaFighter3.exe instead, with Proton forced on), but the native Linux build above is the one to use. The Deck package also keeps a copy of your vf3.zip in your user data folder, so an update unpacked into a new folder doesn't ask for it again.
On another x86-64 Linux PC: unpack it anywhere, put vf3.zip in its roms folder and run VirtuaFighter3.sh.

Portable mode: put a file named portable.txt next to the program (Windows: beside VirtuaFighter3.exe; Mac: beside the app, in the same folder), or in the folder above it, and the game keeps everything in that folder: settings, saves, screenshots, log.txt and the copy of your vf3.zip (in its roms folder), with nothing in your user data folder (%APPDATA%, ~/Library/Application Support). The Linux / Steam Deck build keeps everything in its folder already.

Virtua Fighter 2 (SEGA, arcade, Model 2, 1994) as a native PC game: the game's own i960 program, recompiled to native code, with render scales up to 6x, widescreen and smooth motion at any refresh rate.
Play · Download · Trailer · Status · Controls · Report a bug
The online trailer (click to watch on YouTube)

[!IMPORTANT] No game files are included: no ROMs and nothing made from them. You need your own dump of the game as MAME's vf2 set (vf2.zip, Version 2.1). It is read on your computer, and the game's program is recompiled there each time it starts. An unofficial fan project, not made, approved or supported by SEGA, and not affiliated with it.

Virtua Fighter 2 Recomp runs the game's own program, for the board's Intel i960 CPU, recompiled to native code (ARM64 or x86-64) from your ROM each time it starts, and checked instruction for instruction, cycle for cycle against MAME's i960 interpreter. Only the i960 program is recompiled: the rest of the Model 2A board (the TGP geometry processor, the geometrizer and polygon renderer, the System 24 tile layers, and the sound board's 68000 and SCSP) runs on code from MAME, inside an SDL 3 host. At 1x you get the arcade's frames and sound as MAME makes them (pixel for pixel on Apple silicon…
Menu > Cheats > Player 1 fighter (and Player 2 fighter):

Random: a new fighter every game, made of three of the cast: its head, body and limbs from the three, and its moves dealt from them a move group at a time (its Punch moves one's, its Kick moves another's, its throws a third's, and so on), so it plays like a mix of them, at the game's own timings. Its stance is the first's and its voice one of theirs, and it gets a name made of theirs on the energy bar (JACPAIWOLF, LIJACPAI).

Textures: every part is drawn in its own fighter's textures and their colours, as on that fighter: Jacky's vest, Kage's wraps, Pai's and Lau's patterns, belts, boots and bare feet beside its head's face and hair.

Colours: new every game (not part of a seed). A random fighter wears its head's colours, so its face, hair and skin are right and its skin is one tone all over; its clothes' main colour is turned round the colour wheel, or given a theme: cool, warm, two opposite colours, neon, pastel, black and white, black and gold. Its hair (and headband, hood) is given a hue of its own, as in VF1 Recomp, in the fight and on its select portrait; Shun's white hair and Dural's chrome stay as they are. Belts and shoes keep their colours (VF2 shares those between its fighters).

Seed: type a fighter's name, as seen on an energy bar, to get that fighter again: the same build and the same moves on any machine. A name is the same fighter in every game that has it: VF1 Recomp's 337 names are here with their recipes (the same three, head, voice and moves by group), then VF2's own with Lion or Shun, 678 in all (docs/SEEDS.md; Random draws from the whole book). VF3 Recomp carries this book on in turn (docs/random_book.txt, vf2random --recipes).

Anything but Normal is picked for you at the select, as in VF1 Recomp: playing alone, or with both players random (offline or online), the select is skipped (who you got is a surprise as the fight comes in); beside a player on Normal, it shows, the Normal player picks as ever and the random one is picked at once: its portrait is its head's, and no name is shown under it. A challenger's select doesn't pick again for a player already in, whose portrait is their random fighter's own head and hair in its colours. The attract shows random fighters too: each side whose player has one (Random: new…
The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, running natively on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows and Linux. A static recompilation of the GameCube original, with touch controls, controller support and mods.

[!IMPORTANT] Bring your own disc. BlueWake needs your own legally obtained copy of The Wind Waker for GameCube, USA version (GZLE01, revision 0). This repository contains no disc image, game assets or saves.
On Mac, iPhone, iPad, Linux and Android, the app you build contains code translated from your disc. It is yours alone: never share or upload it.
Questions or bugs? Ask on Discord or open an issue.
Wind Waker Recomp has moved here. Its creator, Elliott, now maintains BlueWake together with Chris, and his work is part of BlueWake with his authorship kept.

Windows: BlueWake's Windows build, on the latest release, is built from BlueWake itself and replaces Wind Waker Recomp 0.4.0. Smooth Motion is off by default (press F10 to turn it on), and 0.4.0's experimental 60 FPS game logic is gone.
Saves carry over: both use %APPDATA%\BlueWake. Back that folder up before switching.
Bugs and requests go to BlueWake's issues. Say which build you use and attach your session log.
How the move happened and what's left of it: migration status.
Download BlueWake-v0.12.0-windows-x64.zip from the latest release. It is ready to play: you don't need PadMint or a Mac.
Unpack the whole ZIP and run BlueWake.exe.
On first launch, choose your disc image (.iso or .gcm). A Dolphin .rvz must first be converted to ISO in Dolphin: right-click the game and choose Convert File.

You need a CPU with AVX2 (Intel Haswell from 2013, AMD Ryzen, or newer) and a Direct3D 12 GPU; since 0.8.0 an older GPU gets Direct3D 11 instead of a black screen (not yet checked on such a PC). If nothing happens when you open it, see the FAQ below. To build it yourself from your disc instead, see BlueWake on Windows.
Download BlueWake-v0.12.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage from the latest release. It is ready to play, and built to run on SteamOS too.
Make it executable (chmod +x, or Properties › Permissions in the Deck's desktop mode) and run it.
On first launch, BlueWake Setup asks for your disc image (.iso or .gcm). --setup opens it again later.

You need an x86-64 CPU with AVX2, a Vulkan driver, and a system with glibc 2.38 or newer, which SteamOS and current distributions have. To build it yourself from your disc instead, see BlueWake on Linux.
a Mac with Apple silicon, Xcode (with the iOS platform installed), and at least 25 GB of free space
an A13 or newer iPhone or iPad on iOS/iPadOS 17 or later, with Developer Mode on
an Apple ID for signing (a free one works, but its apps expire after seven days)

PadMint's GitHub Cloud Build, which makes some other games without a Mac, can't make BlueWake: the build turns code from your own disc into the app, so it has to run on your own Mac. Without one, you can play the Windows or Linux version.

Build your app. The easiest way is PadMint: open it, choose BlueWake and pick your disc. It takes the app from the latest release and adds the game made from your disc. To build from the latest source instead, run this from a checkout of this repository: Expect a first build of well over an hour. Add --source-only first to check your tools and disc in a few minutes. PadMint can also build it on a Windows PC, experimentally; see On a Windows PC.
Install the IPA with Sideloadly, AltStore, SideStore or Xcode. On Windows, Sideloadly.
Copy the same disc image to your device: in Finder on a Mac, or the Apple Devices app on Windows, select the device, open Files and drag it onto BlueWake. The app imports it on first launch.

bloques: This recompilation is a byproduct of developing snesrecomp — the games are the proving ground, the framework is the goal. These are in-development previews, not finished ports — expect rough edges, and depth will keep landing over months, not days. My time for any one title is limited, so I ask for your patience. Contributions are welcome — testing, issues, and PRs to the game or framework all help and will accelerate this game's polish. More on the why at: Recomp + AI: 5 Months Later »

Static recompilation of Super Mario World (SNES) into native C, using the snesrecomp framework. This repo is the per-game side: the runtime, the recompiled C output, the per-game .cfg, and the build glue.

The 65816 CPU code from the ROM is statically translated to C — every function the game runs on the SNES's main CPU is a real generated C function in src/gen/. The rest of the SNES is not recompiled — it's hardware. PPU rendering, the APU / SPC700 audio coprocessor, DMA and HDMA channels, hardware register I/O, and bank-mapping all run through a C reimplementation of the SNES hardware in snesrecomp/runner/src/snes/ — a LakeSnes-derived core (the same emulator family the snesrev reverse-engineered ports use), with individual algorithms credited to snes9x. This is the same model other…
Yoshi's Island (World 1) including Iggy's castle boss.
Vanilla Dome (World 3) in progress at time of writing.

No catastrophic visible regressions surfaced through these worlds. Two runtime tripwires (the M/X claim verifier and the async-cpu->m_flag/x_flag-write detector) are armed at boot and have not latched on the verified worlds. An off-rails event was captured in BufferScrollingTiles_Layer1_VerticalLevel_M1X1 during Donut Plains castle (bank-out-of-range pointer read; runtime mirrors the read to a safe location and gameplay continues) — see ISSUES.md for the bucketed capture and the offrails_get TCP query.

Worlds 4–7 and special content (Star Road, Special World) are not yet hand-verified but are expected to play similarly. If you hit a visible regression, please open an issue with a savestate and the offrails_get / mx_async_check_get JSON snapshots.
Some branches don't build; only main is guaranteed to build.
APIs and recompiler output change without notice.

Download the Windows ZIP or Linux AppImage from Releases. Extract the ZIP, or make the AppImage executable.

Run SuperMarioWorldSNESRecomp.exe or the AppImage. On first launch a file picker asks for your legally-obtained Super Mario World (USA) ROM (.sfc / .smc). The path is remembered in rom.cfg next to the exe.
Edit keybinds.ini (auto-generated next to the exe on first run) to remap keys, then restart.
The ROM is never redistributed — supply your own dump.

To play as Captain Falcon, enable Captain Falcon on the launcher's Mods page, select your Super Smash Bros. (USA) v1.0 ROM, and press Play. The included helper prepares Falcon's assets in your user cache on first use. No Python installation or environment setup is required.

In the launcher's Mods page, enable SMW Playtest Diagnostics → Diagnostic recording. Keep the gameplay mods and settings needed for your reproduction, including native co-op where applicable. Disable run-ahead while recording.

Snap64 Recomp is a native PC port of Pokémon Snap (Nintendo 64, US release) for Windows, Linux, the Steam Deck and macOS. It is made with N64: Recompiled, which translates the game's own code so that it runs directly on a PC. The method is called static recompilation. RT64 draws the picture. A beta of the same port runs on Android phones and handhelds.

Out of the box it plays like the cartridge. Widescreen, higher frame rates, mouse and gyro aim, button rebinding, fast forward, photo export and the Snap Station's printer are there when you want them, and each stays off until you turn it on.

This repository and its releases contain no game assets. You need your own ROM of the US cartridge to play. Only the US cartridge's ROM works: the Japanese, European and Australian releases are different builds of the game, and the port is made from the US one.

[!NOTE] Snap64 Recomp is released only on this repository's Releases page. Copies posted anywhere else are not the project's. On Windows the port is a ZIP holding a folder with Snap64Recomp.exe, and nothing has to be installed. It opens no network connection and asks for no account or password. Each file has a .sha256 beside it, and SECURITY.md says how to check a download.

Contents: Get it running · Screenshots · System requirements · Features · Faithful by default · Controls · Linux and Steam Deck · macOS · Android (beta) · FAQ · Known issues · What's next · Reporting a bug · Contributing · What has been verified · Building · How it was made · Thanks · Documentation · License
The manual has every control, page, hotkey and setting. The rest of the documentation is listed near the end.

In a hurry? The download holds a START HERE.txt with the short version. The one thing to know: this port has no launcher and no overlay. Everything it adds is inside the game's own Options screen. Press Esc, or Select on a pad, and it opens over the screen you are on: the title, the lab, the course map, a paused course. Widescreen, the frame rate and the other enhancements are under Options > Graphics. They all start off, set to what the console did.
These steps are for Windows. Linux and the Steam Deck are further down.
Download Snap64Recomp-1.1.8-win64.zip from the Releases page and unpack it anywhere. It holds one folder, Snap64Recomp-1.1.8-win64, with Snap64Recomp.exe inside. Nothing has to be installed.

Have your ROM of the US cartridge ready. (A ROM is the cartridge's contents, read out into one file.) Put it next to Snap64Recomp.exe with the name pokemonsnap.z64, or just start the program. If no ROM is there, the program asks for the file, checks it, and copies it into place under that name. It only asks once. You do not have to check the file yourself: a wrong one is refused, with a message that says why.

Start Snap64Recomp.exe. The program is not signed, so Windows may first show a "Windows protected your PC" box (SmartScreen). Click "More info", then "Run anyway", and it will not ask again. The first start takes a little longer than later ones, because the renderer builds the shader programs your GPU needs. They are kept in cache/, so the next start is quick.
A few keys to know first:

Esc opens the port's Options on almost any screen, and closes them again. On a pad it is Select. The Graphics and Sound pages are in there. In-game pages in the manual names the few screens where the key does nothing.
Enter is the game's Start. In a course it opens the pause menu: Continue, Quit Course, Retry, Options.
F11 switches fullscreen on and off, in a course or anywhere else. The window's maximize button fills the screen with the window itself, and the port opens it that way again next time.

Sega's 1992 arcade game OutRunners as a native game for computers, the Nintendo Switch, Android and Anbernic's handhelds, built on its decompilation, outrunners-decomp: the game's program in C, checked frame by frame against MAME in picture and sound. Two games come out of it:
OutRunners Arcade: the arcade game as it is, both cabinet screens side by side.
OutRunners: the console version, the arcade game made for playing at home.
This repository contains no game data: you bring your own ROM set (MAME's orunners, World), and the game takes its assets out of it.
REVERSE: the goal picked on the route map">

Download the package for Windows, Linux or macOS from the releases. Keep orunners.zip beside the game, or drop it on its window when it asks: the first time, it takes the assets out of it. --game gives it the set's path (OutRunners --game D:\roms\orunners.zip), for a shortcut; with RecompLauncher you pick orunners.zip once and it does the rest (recomplauncher.json, in each package).

Each device has a package of its own: the game without its assets, and the tool (for Windows, macOS and Linux) that makes it on your computer with your ROM set. Each package's name carries the release's version (outrunners-v1.3.2-windows-x64.zip):
Nintendo Switch (outrunners-VERSION-switch.zip): OutRunners NSP makes OutRunners.nsp, for a console with Atmosphere (ports/switch).
Anbernic's H700 handhelds (outrunners-VERSION-anbernic.zip, RG35XX, RG40XX...): OutRunners Anbernic makes the folder for PORTS (ports/anbernic).
The R36S on ArkOS (outrunners-VERSION-r36s.zip, RK3326, with PortMaster): OutRunners R36S makes the folder for ArkOS's ports (ports/r36s).
What a tool makes has the game's data in it: it is yours alone, never share it.
ARCADE: the arcade's game, one player.
2 PLAYERS: both seats in one race, side by side or one over the other.
NETWORK: up to four devices on the local network (below).
& KNUCKLES: CLASSIC (the arcade's game, a little more time), TIME ATTACK (against your fastest run's ghost), FULL (all 31 courses in one race), REVERSE (from a goal back to the start).

OPTIONS: controls, difficulty, time, video (window, full screen, sharp, smooth or CRT pixels, a wider picture: AUTO, the screen's shape, as a Steam Deck's in its hands or on a TV, or 16:10, 16:9 or 20:9; VSYNC), volume, sound test, steering, FPS.
The radio: > go round its ten songs and Jingle Bell, the hidden one, between Last Wave and Magical Sound Shower.
The pause in a race: CONTINUE, RESTART, QUIT GAME.
The picture: the scenery the arcade draws every other frame to make it look faint (the spray of Niagara's falls, the pyramids) is drawn see-through instead, so it does not blink.
Keyboard: the arrows steer, accelerate and brake; Q and A shift up and down; space is the radio; Enter starts and pauses.
Game controller: the left stick or the d-pad steers, the right trigger accelerates, the left trigger brakes, the shoulders shift. OPTIONS > CONTROLS changes them.

Racing wheel: a wheel SDL knows (a Logitech G29) works as it is plugged in. Any other (a Thrustmaster T300RS) is set up once in OPTIONS > STEERING > SET UP WHEEL: turn the wheel left, press the gas, the brake, and the buttons it asks for; pedals and a shifter plugged in on their own are taken as they are pressed. Also in STEERING: WHEEL ROTATION (your wheel's range: 900 on a G29), CENTRING (the cabinet's spring, on a wheel with force feedback), VIBRATION (the cabinet's wheel shaking in a crash and off the road, or a controller's rumble) and INPUT TEST.

The Oracles Project runs your own ROM of Oracle of Ages or Oracle of Seasons, untouched, in a Game Boy Color emulator core, and adds what the original screen could not show: a widescreen view with the rooms around Link, options that make the game easier to play and to read, languages, mods and four fan games, Oracles Combined among them. Nothing of the game's code is rewritten, so it plays as it always did; docs/ARCHITECTURE.md says how.
Widescreen: Enhanced shows the rooms around Link in the shape of your screen, at three distances, Near, Medium and Far; Faithful keeps the original picture, 160x144, exactly what the game draws.

Easier to play: item hotkeys (four keys that use or equip an item without the menu), swimming with a button held rather than tapped, continuous transitions (Link keeps walking as the screen scrolls), and cheats if you want them (no damage, ammo and rupees that never run out).
Easier to read: a compact text whose letters take their own width, a wider text box, a larger text for small screens, and instant text.
Filters: Scanlines, CRT, LCD (the grid of a Game Boy screen), Smooth, xBR, HQ2x or OmniScale over the game's picture, with a preview as you choose.

Languages: French, German, Italian, Spanish and the European English, taken from your own European ROM; Japanese, from your own Japanese ROM; and Polish, Kaxus's fan translation, from your Polish ROM or his patch.
RetroAchievements, if you want them: log in with your account for achievements on Ages and Seasons' original ROMs, in casual mode, savestates included.
Saves: import a save from another emulator or from the European game; on Android, export a copy to play it elsewhere.
Portable mode: on Windows, and on Linux with the .tar.gz, the settings and mods stay in the game folder, to play from a USB stick or keep several copies side by side.
Lua mods: houses, characters who talk and minigames, which act on the game through the game's own routines and replay exactly.

Fan games from their BPS patch, applied in memory to your ROM: Gifts of Kinomi and Moonrise Regalia on Oracle of Ages, Temple of Seasons on Oracle of Seasons, and Oracles Combined, both Oracles in one, on their two European ROMs.
Two emulator cores: SameBoy, the accurate reference, or mGBA's Game Boy core, lighter, for small devices.

GTA: Vice City Stories — Native PC port (PS2 static recompilation)

A native Windows and Linux port of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories (PS2, USA, SLUS-21590), made by recompiling the game's PS2 executable into C++. Both are built from the same source and run natively: Direct3D 11 on Windows, Vulkan on Linux.

This repository contains no game code or game data. You need your own copy of the game as an .iso. The build reads the executable from your disc, and the finished game reads everything else from it while it runs.
Status: in development. See docs/PROGRESS.md for what works, and docs/LINUX.md for the Linux build in detail.

Download the newest VCS-Recomp- -windows.zip from the Releases page and extract it somewhere short and local, like C:\Games\VCS (not Program Files, not a OneDrive-synced folder such as Desktop or Documents: the build writes thousands of files).
Start VCSLauncher.exe in that folder. It walks you through four steps, one at a time, then shows a big Play button:
Folder: the game is built in build\ next to the launcher, or in a folder you choose (another drive with more room, say): Choose another folder on this step.

Disc: it looks for your .iso in Downloads, Desktop, Documents and its own folder; otherwise choose it (or drag it onto the window, or copy your disc from a DVD drive). It checks that it is the USA release.

Build tools: the game is compiled on your PC with Microsoft's free C++ tools. If they are missing, Install build tools runs Microsoft's installer with the right options (about 6 GB; Windows asks for permission).

Build: recompiles the game from your disc and compiles it, with a progress bar - 20 to 60 minutes the first time, a few minutes after an update. Nothing is downloaded during the build: the release brings Python and the libraries.

The launcher also backs up and restores your saves, makes a desktop shortcut, checks for a new release (only when you ask, or at start if you turn that on in *Settings*), and zips the logs into a report for bug reports. Windows may warn that the launcher is from an unknown publisher (it isn't signed): More info > Run anyway. How it works: docs/LAUNCHER.md. Everything it does is a script in tools/ you can also run yourself (below). If the Pricedown font (GTA's lettering, free for personal desktop use from Typodermic) is installed on your PC, the launcher uses it for its title and Play button…

Download the newest VCS-Recomp- -x86_64.AppImage from the Releases page. It runs on any 64-bit desktop with glibc 2.35 or newer: Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Linux Mint 21, Fedora, Arch and later, on X11 or Wayland. It needs a Vulkan driver (Mesa or NVIDIA's) and python3, which every desktop has.

Make it executable and start it: in the file manager, Properties > Permissions > Allow executing as a program, or chmod +x VCS-Recomp-*.AppImage && ./VCS-Recomp-*.AppImage. The first start puts the game's files (the source, the scripts, the libraries) in ~/.local/share/VCSRecomp/install, where the game is built, then walks you through the same steps as on Windows:
Folder: where the game is built (another drive with more room: *Choose another folder*).
Disc: your .iso from Downloads, Desktop or Documents, chosen, or dropped onto the window.

Build tools: the compiler (clang 19 or newer) and the libraries the build needs, from your distribution. Install packages asks for your password and installs them; Install in a terminal shows the command instead. On Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 12, whose clang is older, it adds LLVM's own repository (apt.llvm.org) first.
